Principles


The eight main points outlined in the Atlantic Charter


These foundational principles were forged in the aftermath of World War II, a time of great upheaval and uncertainty. The Atlantic Charter, a joint statement issued by the United States and the United Kingdom, represented a bold vision for a post-war world. It was a call to action, a promise to work together to build a brighter future for all nations and peoples.


The right of self-determination for all people


This fundamental principle is at the heart of the Atlantic Charter. It recognizes that every individual, every community, and every nation has the inherent right to determine its own destiny. This means that people should be free to choose their own path, to govern themselves, and to build their own futures.


In a world where colonialism and imperialism had long been the norm, the right of self-determination was a revolutionary idea. It was a declaration that people had the power to shape their own lives, to make their own decisions, and to build their own societies.


The commitment to disarmament and collective security


As the world emerged from the devastation of World War II, the need for disarmament and collective security was more pressing than ever. The Atlantic Charter acknowledged that the only way to prevent future wars was to work together to reduce the threat of nuclear war and to build a system of collective security.


This commitment to disarmament and collective security was a bold step towards a more peaceful world. It recognized that the pursuit of national interests and security could no longer be pursued at the expense of global stability and security.


The promotion of economic cooperation and trade


The Atlantic Charter also recognized the importance of economic cooperation and trade in building a more prosperous and stable world. It acknowledged that economic development and growth were essential to the well-being of nations and peoples.


In a world where economic inequality and poverty were rampant, the promotion of economic cooperation and trade was a vital step towards creating a more just and equitable world. It recognized that the free flow of goods, services, and ideas was essential to building a more prosperous and peaceful world.


These principles and provisions, outlined in the Atlantic Charter, continue to shape our world today. They represent a powerful vision for a more just, peaceful, and prosperous world, and they serve as a reminder of the importance of working together to build a better future for all.
